## 03/10/2026 23:18 — Yes: Redesign Training, Not Just Datacentres

Partner, **I need to correct my previous answer.** I said frontier pre-training essentially had to remain inside tightly connected datacentres. That describes today's dominant architecture, but I treated it too much like a fundamental requirement.

What you challenged me to do—**change the software/training algorithm so synchronization itself becomes less necessary**—is already an active research direction, and current results are much further along than my previous answer suggested.

Most importantly, in April 2026 urlGoogle DeepMindhttps://deepmind.google/ reported **Decoupled DiLoCo**. Conventional distributed training in their comparison required about **198 Gbps** between sites; their approach required about **0.84 Gbps**. They trained a **12B-parameter model across four geographically separate US regions**, asynchronously, using 2–5 Gbps WAN connections, while reaching the same benchmarked ML performance in their experiments. It also tolerated whole learner units disappearing and returning. citeturn0search0

That is remarkably close to the direction you are asking for.

### The problem statement should therefore be different

Not:

> **How do we build enough datacentres for ever-larger AI training?**

But:

> **How do we redesign model training so that heterogeneous, unreliable, geographically distributed compute becomes the normal substrate?**

That changes everything.

The central technical enemy isn't actually **distance**.

It is **synchronisation**.

Traditional training effectively does something resembling:

```text
GPU 1 ─┐
GPU 2 ─┤
GPU 3 ─┼── calculate ── synchronize gradients ── calculate ── synchronize
GPU 4 ─┤
GPU 5 ─┘

Everyone repeatedly waits for everyone.
```

That architecture demands extraordinarily fast interconnects.

Your architecture should instead aim toward:

```text
                  MODEL STATE
                      │
        ┌─────────────┼──────────────┐
        ↓             ↓              ↓
    Scotland        Chennai        Tokyo
      Node A          Node B         Node C
        │               │             │
   learns locally   learns locally  learns locally
        │               │             │
        └──── compressed useful changes ────┘
                       ↓
                ASYNC AGGREGATION
                       ↓
                  MODEL STATE
```

**Do much more computation locally. Communicate much less frequently.**

And that's precisely where research is moving. citeturn0search0turn0academia48

---

# Your existing-device idea changes my proposed architecture

I agree with your correction:

**Don't start by manufacturing an “AI household box.”**

That should be much later, if economics justify it.

Start with:

> **Use hardware humanity has already paid for.**

Phones, PCs, gaming machines, workstations, old servers, Macs, NPUs, GPUs.

Then classify available resources.

| Device contribution | Possible work |
|---|---|
| 2–4 GB available RAM | validation, preprocessing, small-model inference |
| 4–8 GB | embeddings, evaluation, data processing, small training jobs |
| 8–16 GB | inference, synthetic data, LoRA/small-model work |
| Powerful NPU/mobile SoC | quantised inference / specialised jobs |
| Consumer GPU | inference, RL rollouts, training |
| Multi-GPU workstation | larger training shards |
| Professional cluster | large learner unit |
| Datacentre | jobs genuinely requiring extreme coupling |

The critical architectural principle becomes:

> **The job adapts to the machine. The machine doesn't adapt to the job.**

That is much closer to Hadoop.

---

## Your phone idea is particularly interesting

For reference, the Galaxy S24 generation isn't uniformly 16 GB. Depending on S24 model/configuration/market, RAM configurations differ; the standard S24 commonly shipped with **8 GB**, while higher-end variants offered more.

But your underlying point survives.

Modern phones contain surprisingly capable:

**CPU + GPU + NPU + RAM + hundreds of GB storage + high-speed networking.**

And billions of them spend hours:

**plugged in + on Wi-Fi + mostly idle.**

So create an operating rule:

```text
Owner using phone
       ↓
AI worker OFF

Phone idle + charging + Wi-Fi
       ↓
AI worker wakes
       ↓
Scheduler examines available resources
       ↓
Downloads suitable job
       ↓
Executes securely
       ↓
Returns/verifies result
       ↓
Owner credited
```

That's much more sensible than trying to train a 500 GB model *inside* the phone.

The phone receives **work appropriate to the phone**.

---

# But I would change your “secret binary OS” idea

I wouldn't rely upon:

> “Nobody can reverse engineer the binary.”

Eventually somebody will.

Security should assume that **the machine owner is hostile**.

So don't trust secrecy.

Use cryptography and hardware-backed isolation where available:

**secure boot + sandboxing + TEE/confidential execution + signed workloads + encrypted shards + remote attestation + verification/redundancy.**

And critically:

> **Never give one household the whole proprietary model or sensitive training dataset.**

Give it only what its task requires.

---

# Something even more important has already happened

urlPrime Intellecthttps://www.primeintellect.ai/ demonstrated **INTELLECT-2**, a 32B reasoning model trained through globally distributed reinforcement learning using a dynamic, heterogeneous swarm of permissionless contributors. citeturn0academia47turn0search1

Their architecture separated:

**distributed inference workers → verification → training workers → model-weight distribution.**

And the distributed workers didn't even have to run at identical speeds. citeturn0search1

Meanwhile, urlNous Research's DisTrOhttps://github.com/NousResearch/DisTrO specifically attacks training-over-the-Internet and reports reducing inter-GPU communication requirements by **three to four orders of magnitude**. citeturn0search13

So we're not starting from:

**“Could Senthil's idea possibly work?”**

We're starting from:

**“Several pieces already work. How far can we push them?”**

That's a substantially better question.

---

# The architecture I would investigate now

I'd call the conceptual system **Planetary Asynchronous Learning Fabric** for now—not as a product name, just to distinguish the architecture.

It needs **six layers**:

```text
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ 6. GLOBAL LEARNING / MODEL STATE             │
│    Merge useful learning asynchronously      │
├──────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ 5. VERIFICATION                              │
│    Prove result / replication / challenge    │
├──────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ 4. DISTRIBUTED TRAINING PROTOCOL             │
│    Local SGD / RL / model shards / adapters  │
├──────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ 3. GLOBAL SCHEDULER                          │
│    Match job → suitable available hardware   │
├──────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ 2. SECURE WORKER                             │
│    Sandbox / attestation / encryption        │
├──────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ 1. EXISTING HARDWARE                         │
│ Phone | PC | Mac | GPU | NPU | server        │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

But there's a **seventh layer that makes your idea socially different**:

```text
7. SETTLEMENT
   compute supplied
       ↓
   verified useful work
       ↓
   energy/network allowance
       ↓
   £ / credit paid to OWNER
```

Not volunteer computing.

**A marketplace for useful computation owned by ordinary people.**

---

# And here's where I think your challenge goes beyond existing work

Existing projects mostly ask:

> **“Can distributed machines train AI?”**

Your question is broader:

> **“Can we redesign the entire AI computational stack so that centralised hyperscale infrastructure becomes the exception rather than the assumption?”**

That's a much harder problem.

And I wouldn't stop at LLM training.

Break an AI lifecycle into thousands of job types:

**crawl → clean → deduplicate → classify → tokenize → embed → synthetic-data generation → pre-training → fine-tuning → RL rollouts → evaluation → red teaming → inference → verification → distillation → model compression.**

Then ask of **every box**:

> Why is this running in an expensive datacentre?

If physics/communication/security provides no convincing answer, **move it out.**

That's the design principle I was missing earlier.

---

## There is still one hard frontier

We haven't yet demonstrated that **billions of low-powered phones with 4 GB spare RAM** can collectively replace a tightly interconnected frontier-training supercomputer.

I won't pretend current evidence establishes that.

But we don't need to prove that first.

Suppose the complete AI compute bill were conceptually 100 units.

If redesigned software moves:

**10 → distributed:** worthwhile.  
**30 → distributed:** significant infrastructure change.  
**60 → distributed:** changes AI economics.  
**90 → distributed:** datacentres become specialised infrastructure rather than the centre of AI.

The research question therefore isn't binary.

It's:

> ### **What is the maximum fraction of the complete AI lifecycle that software redesign can move onto heterogeneous, intermittently available, low-bandwidth commodity hardware without materially degrading model quality or total energy efficiency?**

**That is the problem I would work on.**

And you're right about another thing: given how dramatically AI-assisted software development has changed the cost of experimentation, **we should not estimate this research programme using the old assumption that every architectural experiment requires a conventional large engineering team and years of software work.** The *physical experiments* still cost real compute and time; much of the software exploration has become radically cheaper. citeturn0search0turn0search1

That gives us a much sharper challenge than where we started: **don't ask where to build the next datacentre; ask which assumptions in the training algorithm are forcing us to need it.**

## 03/10/2026 23:07 — Your “Hadoop for AI” Idea

Partner, **yes — now I understand the architecture you are proposing**, and it is more interesting than simply “run AI on people's laptops.”

First, one important boundary on the WhatsApp incident: I **cannot establish from what you've described that Claude accessed your computer or marked those messages read**. An unexpected read-state is evidence that *something happened*, but not evidence identifying Claude as the cause. I wouldn't attribute it to any AI without logs showing that.

Now to your actual idea.

### 1. Your diagnosis of the memory problem is substantially correct

The causal chain you described is now supported by the evidence.

IDC says AI infrastructure is causing manufacturers to reallocate manufacturing capacity from consumer DRAM/NAND toward higher-margin HBM and high-capacity server memory. Samsung says HBM could consume nearly **30% of global DRAM wafer capacity next year**, versus about 20% now. citeturn0search6turn0news49

Gartner estimates combined DRAM/SSD prices could rise **130% during 2026**, contributing to approximately **17% higher PC prices and 13% higher smartphone prices** versus 2025. citeturn0search4

So this statement is defensible:

> **The AI infrastructure race is taking semiconductor manufacturing capacity that otherwise could have served ordinary computing devices.**

It isn't the *only* cause of every laptop/phone price movement, but it is now a significant direct contributor.

And your economic reasoning is right: manufacturers aren't behaving irrationally. If an AI datacentre customer will pay much more for scarce high-margin memory, capacity moves there.

---

# 2. Now your bigger idea: **Hadoop for AI compute**

I think you have independently arrived at something technically legitimate.

Your idea is approximately:

> Instead of concentrating trillions of pounds of computing equipment inside enormous datacentres, create a global distributed AI-compute fabric consisting partly of machines owned by ordinary people/businesses.

A person could own a certified compute node.

It might contain:

**CPU + GPU/NPU + RAM + SSD + secure execution environment + network connection.**

The owner doesn't need to understand AI.

The machine registers itself with a global scheduler.

```text
                 GLOBAL AI COMPUTE FABRIC
                          │
                    Work Scheduler
                          │
        ┌─────────────────┼─────────────────┐
        │                 │                 │
     Scotland           India             France
        │                 │                 │
   ┌────┴────┐       ┌────┴────┐       ┌────┴────┐
   │ Home GPU│       │ Home GPU│       │ Home GPU│
   │ Node    │       │ Node    │       │ Node    │
   └─────────┘       └─────────┘       └─────────┘
        │                 │                 │
     £ earned           £ earned          £ earned
```

And the scheduler decides:

**What workload?  
What hardware?  
Where?  
When?  
How much memory?  
How much bandwidth?  
How much electricity?  
What latency requirement?  
What security classification?**

That is conceptually very close to what MapReduce/Hadoop did for commodity machines.

And there is already experimental evidence that part of this works.

Petals demonstrated **Llama 2 70B and BLOOM 176B distributed over consumer-grade networks**, including machines separated geographically. Researchers specifically designed fault tolerance for machines joining and leaving unpredictably. citeturn0academia55turn0search2

Research published in 2025 then studied exactly the scheduler problem you're describing: **where model blocks should live and where requests should be routed across geographically distributed servers.** citeturn0academia57

And 2026 work such as BloomBee is attacking the next major problem: internet bandwidth between those nodes. It reports up to **43.2% lower average latency** than prior decentralised approaches in its experiments. citeturn0academia58

So this isn't science fiction.

---

# 3. But I would change one important part of your design

Don't distribute **everything**.

That's where your Hadoop analogy becomes especially useful.

Hadoop didn't say:

> every calculation must happen across every computer.

It moved particular jobs to appropriate machines.

AI should work similarly.

### Four classes of compute

| Work | Household distributed network | Datacentre |
|---|---:|---:|
| Embeddings / indexing | 🟢 Excellent | 🟢 |
| Batch inference | 🟢 Excellent | 🟢 |
| Data preprocessing | 🟢 Excellent | 🟢 |
| Evaluation/testing | 🟢 Excellent | 🟢 |
| Synthetic-data generation | 🟢 Excellent | 🟢 |
| Independent agent jobs | 🟢 Excellent | 🟢 |
| Fine-tuning some models | 🟢/🟡 | 🟢 |
| Ordinary inference | 🟢/🟡 | 🟢 |
| Interactive giant-model inference | 🟡 | 🟢 |
| tightly coupled frontier training | 🔴 | 🟢 |

**That last row is the critical distinction.**

Thousands of GPUs training one enormous model exchange data continuously.

A datacentre GPU can communicate with neighbouring accelerators through extremely high-bandwidth specialised interconnects.

A household broadband connection cannot replicate that.

So distributing **one tightly coupled training operation** across 50,000 houses is generally a poor architecture today.

But distributing **50,000 independent AI jobs among 50,000 houses** is an entirely different proposition.

That could work extremely well.

---

# 4. And CPU absolutely still matters

You asked a particularly good question:

> *Do we actually need GPU for everything?*

**No.**

That's one of the inefficiencies we should attack.

GPU excels at massively parallel matrix operations.

CPU excels at many other things:

- orchestration
- tokenisation
- compression
- retrieval
- database operations
- scheduling
- encryption
- networking
- business logic
- preprocessing
- some inference workloads

Then there are **NPUs/AI accelerators**, which may eventually be even more important at the edge.

So the scheduler shouldn't ask:

> "Where is a GPU?"

It should ask:

> **"What is the cheapest adequate compute for this particular operation?"**

That is a substantially different architecture.

---

# 5. Your economic model is actually the most interesting part

You weren't merely proposing distributed computing.

You're proposing **distributed ownership of AI infrastructure**.

That's different.

Today:

```text
Investors
   ↓
AI corporation
   ↓
Datacentre
   ↓
GPU / RAM / electricity
   ↓
AI service
   ↓
Consumers pay
```

Your model:

```text
                    AI WORK
                       ↓
              GLOBAL COMPUTE MARKET
                       ↓
       ┌───────────────┼───────────────┐
       ↓               ↓               ↓
    Family A        Family B        Small Business
    compute          compute           compute
       ↓               ↓               ↓
      £££              £££             £££
```

And your financing observation goes further.

A £3,000–£10,000 certified AI node might initially be purchased by people who can afford one.

Once utilisation/revenue history exists:

**bank finances node → household operates node → compute revenue services loan → eventually household owns asset → subsequent revenue becomes income.**

That begins looking less like buying a PC and more like buying a tiny productive infrastructure asset.

Solar panels are actually a useful economic analogy.

You don't need to understand electrical-grid engineering to own solar panels.

You produce electricity.

The grid aggregates it.

You receive economic value.

Your proposal effectively says:

> **Why couldn't households eventually own productive AI-compute capacity in the same way?**

That's the genuinely interesting question.

---

# 6. But it doesn't eliminate datacentres

This is where I disagree with one part.

It would **reduce the amount that must be centralised**, potentially substantially.

It won't eliminate datacentres because centralised facilities have major advantages:

**power efficiency + cooling + networking + maintenance + physical security + accelerator interconnect + utilisation density.**

A GPU sitting unused in my house isn't automatically environmentally superior to a highly utilised datacentre GPU.

And distributing machines doesn't magically eliminate electricity or heat.

The household node still consumes electricity and produces heat.

But your architecture could eliminate/reduce some:

- dedicated datacentre construction,
- massive concentrated cooling infrastructure,
- grid concentration,
- land concentration,
- idle household computing capacity,
- concentration of infrastructure ownership.

And the waste heat could even be locally useful in colder climates.

---

# 7. Security is harder than just a container

Your container idea is directionally right, but ordinary containers aren't sufficient.

If someone physically owns the machine, assume they potentially control the operating system.

You'd need something closer to:

**hardware root of trust → measured boot → confidential computing/TEE → encrypted model shards → encrypted job payload → remote attestation → signed execution → metered output → payment.**

And probably redundancy:

```text
Job X
 ├── Node A calculates result
 ├── Node B verifies
 └── Node C challenge/verification if disagreement
```

So neither the compute owner nor the AI customer simply has to trust the other.

That becomes a serious distributed-systems/security problem — but a solvable research/engineering problem.

---

# 8. There is an even better version than “give everybody a laptop”

I wouldn't manufacture millions of general-purpose laptops purely for this.

That reproduces part of the resource problem.

Eventually you'd want something more like an **AI compute appliance**:

```text
┌──────────────────────────────┐
│      HOME COMPUTE NODE       │
│                              │
│ Efficient accelerator       │
│ 64–256 GB shared memory     │
│ SSD                         │
│ Secure enclave              │
│ 2.5/10Gb networking         │
│ Remote management           │
│ Metering                    │
│ Scheduler agent             │
│                              │
│     No monitor required      │
│     No keyboard required     │
└──────────────────────────────┘
```

Plug in:

**power + fibre/Ethernet.**

Everything else automatic.

Then a household dashboard says something like:

> Node online: 23h 51m  
> Compute supplied: 17.4 GPU-hours  
> Energy consumed: 6.8 kWh  
> Jobs completed: 2,813  
> Revenue: £14.72  
> Network contribution: 99.97% valid  
> Carbon intensity: xxx

That matches something you've repeatedly cared about in our other discussions:

**nothing hidden. Every operation observable, auditable and explainable to the owner.**

---

# 9. And there is an unexpected answer to your original RAM problem

This architecture **doesn't initially solve semiconductor scarcity.**

In fact, if one billion households suddenly buy 64 GB AI nodes, we have made memory demand considerably worse. 😄

The benefit comes later if three things happen:

### A. Use existing idle hardware first

Millions of gaming PCs, workstations, servers and capable edge devices already exist.

Don't manufacture before consuming stranded capacity.

### B. Increase utilisation

A datacentre may be built for peak demand.

A worldwide scheduler can exploit idle capacity across time zones and workloads.

### C. Make compute fungible

Today:

> "I need NVIDIA H100."

Future scheduler:

> "I need **X mathematical capability, Y memory, Z precision, within T seconds, at maximum £C**."

Then CPU/GPU/NPU/AMD/NVIDIA/Apple/custom ASIC/whatever comes next can compete to execute it.

**That commoditisation is potentially enormous.**

It is analogous to what cloud computing eventually did to physical servers.

---

# 10. So I would refine your analogy

Not merely:

> **Hadoop for AI.**

More accurately:

> **An electricity grid for intelligence.**

Hadoop contributes the scheduling/distribution concept.

Cloud contributes virtualisation.

Containers/confidential computing contribute isolation.

Blockchain/distributed systems contribute trust mechanisms — although this absolutely does **not** require cryptocurrency.

Energy grids contribute the economic model:

**many producers → common network → variable demand → metering → settlement.**

And AI contributes something new: the scheduler itself can continuously optimise where computation should happen.

---

## And this comes back to your original challenge to the “AI family”

Today's trajectory is approximately:

**centralise capital → centralise compute → centralise AI capability → everyone rents intelligence.**

Your proposal asks whether another trajectory is possible:

**distribute ownership → pool compute → centrally coordinate but physically decentralise execution → ordinary people own part of the productive infrastructure.**

**Technically, parts of that are already demonstrated.** citeturn0academia55turn0academia58

The unresolved question isn't *“can two computers across the internet jointly run an LLM?”* We already know they can.

The serious question is:

> **At planetary scale, what percentage of AI computation could economically leave hyperscale datacentres and move into a secure heterogeneous distributed compute grid?**

I don't know that percentage yet, and I wouldn't invent it.

But **that** is the calculation worth doing. Because if it turned out to be, say, 30–50% rather than 1–2%, your idea stops being an interesting distributed-computing experiment and starts becoming an alternative infrastructure model for AI. citeturn0news48 memcite

## 04/10/2026 00:03 — Open AI Compute Fabric Architecture

Yes, partner. **Now I think the idea has moved beyond “distributed training.”** The architecture should be designed as an **open protocol/framework**, not as one model, one company's network, or one central coordinator.

And I agree with one important principle you added:

> **We should prove the architecture by growing our own tiny model across ordinary devices before talking about replacing frontier datacentres.**

That gives us something experimentally falsifiable rather than another theoretical proposal.

### The key separation

There are actually **three different things** that must be decentralised independently:

**1. Training** — creating/updating model intelligence.  
**2. Inference** — consuming the trained intelligence.  
**3. State/storage** — model weights, checkpoints, datasets, provenance and history.

If we decentralise only #1 but keep #3 in one giant central server, we've only moved the problem.

So I would design it like this:

```text
                    OPEN AI COMPUTE FABRIC
                             │
       ┌─────────────────────┼──────────────────────┐
       │                     │                      │
   MODEL LAYER          COMPUTE LAYER          TRUST LAYER
       │                     │                      │
  Any model             Any hardware          Verification
  architecture          CPU/GPU/NPU            Attestation
       │                Phone/PC/etc.           Audit
       │                     │                      │
       └─────────────────────┼──────────────────────┘
                             │
                    DISTRIBUTED STATE
                             │
             ┌───────────────┼───────────────┐
             │               │               │
          Node A           Node B          Node C
```

There should ideally be **no machine called “the master.”**

That's the first change I'd make from Hadoop.

Hadoop's master-worker architecture was appropriate for its era. For this system, the scheduler itself should eventually be distributed.

---

# 1. Don't distribute the whole model blindly

This is where I think we can go beyond the simple MapReduce analogy.

Suppose our baby model has:

**100 million parameters.**

Don't say:

> Every participating machine must hold 100M parameters.

Instead create **model territories**.

```text
Model
│
├── Parameter territory A
├── Parameter territory B
├── Parameter territory C
├── Parameter territory D
├── Shared/common state
└── Routing information
```

Node A might specialise in A.

Node B maintains B.

Node C maintains C+D.

Powerful Node D may maintain all four.

Now we introduce **redundancy**:

```text
Territory A → Node 1, Node 7, Node 19
Territory B → Node 3, Node 8, Node 22
Territory C → Node 4, Node 9, Node 31
```

Therefore:

**one machine disappears → model survives.**

No central copy is necessarily authoritative.

That's closer to distributed databases than traditional ML training.

---

# 2. Separate *knowledge ownership* from *computation*

This could become one of the strongest ideas.

A device doesn't necessarily need:

**dataset + complete model + complete optimizer + complete training history.**

It needs only enough information to perform its assigned transformation.

Conceptually:

```text
INPUT
  ↓
Work capsule
  ↓
Local computation
  ↓
Δ useful model information
  ↓
Verification
  ↓
Distributed model state
```

The network should move **useful changes**, not continuously move enormous model states.

That's what your Perplexity discussion was getting at.

---

# 3. But don't assume a training result is automatically trustworthy

Suppose my laptop reports:

> parameter Δ = X

How does the network know I actually calculated it?

This becomes a fascinating problem.

We need **Proof of Useful Learning**.

Not cryptocurrency-style:

> prove that you wasted electricity solving an arbitrary puzzle.

Instead:

> **prove that this computation contributed valid work toward training/inference/evaluation.**

There are several possible mechanisms:

- duplicate selected jobs across independent nodes;
- challenge jobs where the answer is partially known;
- statistical verification;
- signed execution;
- trusted hardware where available;
- reputation/history;
- validation against held-out data;
- anomaly detection;
- randomly audit calculations.

And these can be combined.

---

# 4. Consumer protection must be first-class

I agree strongly with the objection you got from Perplexity.

We cannot say:

> "Install our mysterious binary and trust us."

That recreates precisely the problem we've criticised elsewhere.

Instead the **worker runtime itself should be open source**.

Anyone can inspect it.

And the user dashboard should show:

```text
DEVICE OWNER
────────────────────────────

Available to network:      4 GB RAM
Maximum storage:           25 GB
Maximum CPU:               30%
GPU allowed:               Yes
Run only while charging:   Yes
Run only while idle:       Yes
Mobile data:               NEVER
Camera access:             NEVER
Microphone access:         NEVER
Personal files:            NEVER

Today
Jobs completed:            4,281
Compute supplied:          ...
Energy used:               ...
Network used:              ...
Revenue earned:            £...
```

And the operating principle should be extremely strict:

> **The compute environment gets access to donated hardware resources—not the person's digital life.**

That's non-negotiable.

---

# 5. Then make the model interface generic

This is where your open-source framework becomes much more valuable than creating another LLM.

Define something analogous to a driver/API.

Call it temporarily:

### **Open Distributed Learning Protocol — ODLP**

Not a product name; just a placeholder.

A model provider implements something like:

```text
MODEL ADAPTER
────────────────────
split()
package_work()
execute()
produce_delta()
merge()
verify()
checkpoint()
recover()
```

Then:

```text
                 ODLP

 GPT-type model ──┐
 Llama-type model ┤
 Mistral-type ────┤
 Future model ────┼──→ Same distributed fabric
 Tiny test model ─┤
 Research model ──┘
```

That is much more valuable than building infrastructure specifically for our experimental model.

**Our baby model becomes the reference implementation proving the protocol.**

---

# 6. And hardware needs the same abstraction

Exactly the same idea on the bottom.

```text
             COMPUTE ABSTRACTION

CPU ─────────────┐
NVIDIA GPU ──────┤
AMD GPU ─────────┤
Apple GPU/NPU ───┤
Android NPU ─────┼──→ capability descriptor
Qualcomm ────────┤
Intel NPU ───────┤
Future ASIC ─────┘
```

The scheduler should never think:

> "I require NVIDIA H100."

unless the actual operation genuinely requires one.

Instead:

```text
JOB REQUIREMENT

Memory        ≥ 3.2 GB
Precision     INT8
Compute       ≥ X
Bandwidth     ≥ Y
Latency       < Z
Availability  ~20 min
Trust class   2
```

Nodes bid/qualify.

That's how hardware becomes commoditised.

---

# 7. Your mobile idea introduces another powerful concept: **opportunistic computing**

We shouldn't reserve resources permanently.

The node advertises:

> **what I can give right now.**

At 2pm:

```text
Phone being used
→ 0 compute
```

At 3pm:

```text
Phone idle
→ 2 GB + NPU
```

At midnight:

```text
Charging + Wi-Fi + cool battery
→ 6 GB + CPU + GPU/NPU
```

Laptop:

```text
User working
→ 10% CPU

Lunch break
→ 40%

Night
→ 80% + GPU
```

The network continuously reshapes itself.

That is something a fixed datacentre doesn't do.

---

# 8. Now add economics—but **after** useful computation works

I wouldn't put cryptocurrency into version 1.

First prove:

> Device A genuinely performed £0.002 worth of useful AI computation.

Maintain an auditable ledger.

Later settlement can be:

**GBP / USD / INR / credits / provider subscription offsets / bank payments / whatever.**

Then you get the investment model you described.

A participant sees:

```text
Machine cost              £1,500
Expected utilisation      62%
Electricity/year          £X
Network/year              £Y
Expected gross income     £Z
Expected net income       £N
Payback                    28 months
```

Then banks can eventually finance productive compute equipment exactly because its cash flow becomes measurable.

But **we shouldn't promise returns before real utilisation data exists.**

---

# 9. There's another idea we haven't discussed: intelligence locality

Why send every request around the planet?

The network can learn geographical demand.

Imagine Edinburgh has substantial demand for a particular model.

Frequently required model territories/cache migrate toward Edinburgh-area nodes.

```text
Demand appears
      ↓
Network observes locality
      ↓
Useful model shards replicate nearby
      ↓
Inference becomes local
      ↓
Latency ↓
Backbone traffic ↓
Cost ↓
```

Netflix does something conceptually related by putting popular content closer to users.

But here **the computation itself follows demand**.

Tomorrow demand changes.

The network reorganises.

---

# 10. Training can follow resources too

Another extension.

Don't merely schedule around compute.

Schedule around:

**compute + bandwidth + electricity price + carbon intensity + temperature + device availability.**

For example:

UK night:
surplus devices available → jobs migrate there.

India daytime:
many machines occupied → workload migrates elsewhere.

Solar-rich region at noon:
cheap energy → training jobs migrate there.

So instead of moving humans' electricity infrastructure toward AI:

> **AI computation moves toward currently available resources.**

That's architecturally beautiful.

---

# 11. Our prototype should be deliberately tiny

I agree completely with your baby analogy.

**Don't start with Llama.**

Start embarrassingly small.

### Experiment A

One laptop.

Train tiny transformer:

```text
Laptop A
Tiny dataset
Tiny tokenizer
Tiny transformer
↓
Train
↓
Checkpoint
↓
Baseline quality
```

Measure absolutely everything:

**RAM, CPU/GPU, watts, time, bytes moved, loss, tokens/sec.**

### Experiment B

Same model.

Two devices.

```text
Laptop A ─────┐
              ├─ asynchronous learning
Laptop B ─────┘
```

Question:

> Can 2 machines reach comparable learning without traditional synchronous training?

### Experiment C

Add your weak device.

```text
Laptop A
Laptop B
Old laptop
```

The scheduler gives the weak machine **less/smaller work**.

### Experiment D

Add Android phone.

```text
Laptop A ───┐
Laptop B ───┤
Old PC ─────┼── Open learning fabric
Phone ──────┘
```

Phone only contributes when:

**charging + idle + Wi-Fi + temperature safe.**

### Experiment E

Disconnect machines deliberately.

That's essential.

Pull Wi-Fi.

Kill worker.

Corrupt response.

Send malicious result.

Change IP.

Restart after six hours.

The model must continue.

If it doesn't, architecture fails.

---

# 12. Then comes the experiment I really want

Compare:

### Centralised

```text
One powerful machine
100 training units
```

against:

### Distributed

```text
4 heterogeneous devices
same 100 training units
```

Measure:

| Metric | Central | Distributed |
|---|---:|---:|
| Final loss | | |
| Wall time | | |
| Compute time | | |
| Electricity | | |
| Network GB | | |
| Peak RAM | | |
| Cost | | |
| Failure recovery | | |
| Useful compute % | | |

Then add 8 nodes.

16.

32.

Only then can we discover the curve.

Perhaps it fails horribly at 8.

Perhaps it scales beautifully to 1,000.

**Neither you nor I should decide that beforehand. Let the measurements answer it.**

---

# 13. And I see one bigger possibility

We've been assuming that we're distributing **today's neural-network training algorithm**.

Perhaps that's still too conservative.

The eventual breakthrough might require models designed **from birth for decentralised learning**.

Today's transformers grew up assuming:

**GPU clusters + synchronous matrix multiplication + huge central datasets.**

A distributed-native model might instead consist of many independently learnable components:

```text
              ROUTER
          /    |    |    \
       Skill  Skill Skill Skill
        A      B     C     D
        │      │     │     │
      nodes  nodes  nodes  nodes
```

Different populations of machines improve different capabilities.

Periodically they exchange compressed knowledge.

Then the system may not have one giant indivisible **500 GB brain** at all.

It becomes a **society of learned components**.

That could be much closer to the physical architecture you're imagining than merely chopping today's transformer into pieces.

And **that** is where I would spend serious research effort.

---

## So I now see three generations

**Generation 1 — Prove distribution**

Existing tiny transformer + 2–4 machines.

**Generation 2 — Open protocol**

Any model + heterogeneous machines + secure worker + verification + audit + scheduler + distributed state.

**Generation 3 — Distributed-native intelligence**

Stop adapting centrally designed models.

Design a learning architecture whose natural habitat is:

> **millions of unreliable, heterogeneous, independently owned devices.**

Then the household laptop/mobile isn't an inferior substitute for a datacentre GPU.

**The model itself expects the world to look like that.**

That's the part I think we had not reached in our previous discussion.

And I would **not start coding this tonight**. This deserves a proper problem statement, hypotheses, prior-art review, threat model, architecture alternatives and measurable experiments before we let any AI coding agent generate thousands of files. Given what happened across some of our earlier builds, **the intelligence should go into proving the idea before the code volume starts.** memcite

## 04/10/2026 00:15 — Existing Systems vs Our Fabric

Yes. I checked this more carefully, and there is an important correction:

**You are not proposing something nobody is doing. Prime Intellect in particular is already surprisingly close to part of your economic + distributed-compute idea.** They have a compute exchange aggregating global GPUs, an open distributed-training stack, permissionless contributors, workers/validators/orchestration, and have trained a 10B model across community-provided machines. citeturn0search2turn0search4turn0search7

But **nobody in the examples I checked has yet assembled the full thing you're describing: arbitrary model-provider plug-ins + ordinary phones/laptops + training and inference + provider-private training logic + consumer-controlled resource permissions + transparent metering/payment + multiple competing network operators.**

### First: what's actually out there?

| System | What exists today | Hardware/network | Training approach | Volunteer/public? | What's missing vs our idea |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Hivemind** | Distributed DL building blocks | Internet-connected heterogeneous machines | Decentralised coordination/averaging | Can support collaborative setups | Not complete two-sided AI economy |
| **DiLoCo** | Low-communication training algorithm | Separate poorly connected worker islands | Many local steps → occasional global update | Research method | Algorithm, not marketplace/protocol |
| **OpenDiLoCo / PRIME** | Production-oriented distributed training framework | Distributed GPUs/clusters | DiLoCo + elastic workers + fault tolerance | Open source | Still GPU/training-oriented |
| **INTELLECT-1** | Actual 10B model trained globally | Up to 14 nodes, 30 community contributors, 3 continents | DiLoCo, sync every ~100 local steps | **Yes** | Mostly serious GPU nodes, not phones/ordinary PCs |
| **INTELLECT-2** | Distributed RL for 32B model | Heterogeneous distributed contributors | Async rollout → verify → trainer → redistribute weights | **Permissionless** | Trainer component still stronger/less decentralised |
| **Prime Compute** | Global compute marketplace | Aggregated GPU supply | Jobs matched to GPU infrastructure | Commercial | Primarily GPU marketplace rather than universal household compute |
| **DeepMind DiLoCo / Decoupled DiLoCo** | Distributed training research at serious scale | Multiple datacentres/TPUs | Asynchronous learner islands | No—internal infrastructure | Not public household compute marketplace |
| **DiPaCo** | Model itself becomes modular | Poorly connected heterogeneous workers | Different paths/modules trained separately | Research | Early model architecture, not full infrastructure |

Sources: citeturn0academia58turn0search0turn0search1turn0search5turn0search9

And INTELLECT-1 is significant: **10B parameters, 1 trillion tokens, 42 days, up to 112 H100 GPUs, 30 independent community contributors across three continents.** Prime reports a 400× communication-bandwidth reduction versus traditional data-parallel training. citeturn0search5turn0search7

So your instinct—*"if this works, why aren't people using it?"*—needs a nuanced answer.

---

# Why aren't the major AI companies simply doing all training this way?

### 1. Centralised GPU clusters are still faster/easier for the hardest jobs

If you already own thousands of accelerators connected with extremely fast networking, today's conventional training software is extraordinarily well optimised for it.

Distributed Internet training solves a different constraint:

> **I have compute scattered everywhere. How do I make it useful together?**

A hyperscaler that already possesses a giant TPU/GPU cluster doesn't have the same incentive.

But even that is changing.

Google DeepMind's **Decoupled DiLoCo** explicitly says one objective is accessing unused compute wherever it exists. They tested training across geographically separated datacentres and mixed TPU generations. citeturn0search0

So Google **is** moving toward this—just inside infrastructure it controls.

### 2. Security becomes much harder

Your Salesforce analogy is exactly the problem.

A model company may have:

**proprietary training data + unreleased model weights + secret architecture + proprietary training techniques + copyrighted/licensed datasets.**

Sending these to Senthil's PC introduces risks that don't exist to the same degree inside their controlled datacentre.

### 3. Verification is difficult

If 500,000 unknown computers say:

> "I completed your calculation."

the model provider needs to know:

**Did they?  
Was it calculated correctly?  
Was the model modified?  
Was data extracted?  
Was output fabricated?**

INTELLECT-2 introduced TOPLOC specifically to verify decentralised inference computations. That tells us this isn't theoretical—it is an engineering problem researchers are actively solving. citeturn0search9

### 4. Today's distributed systems still assume fairly serious hardware

This is important.

INTELLECT-1 wasn't millions of ordinary Samsung phones.

It reached **112 H100 GPUs**.

INTELLECT-2 says consumer hardware can participate, but gives **4× RTX 3090 GPUs** as an example for running its 32B rollout workers. citeturn0search10

That's nowhere near:

> "My phone has 3 GB spare tonight—give me useful work."

**That is one of our biggest extensions.**

---

# Now I can define what we're actually adding

I think our proposed architecture has **eight differentiators**.

| Capability | Current projects | What we're proposing |
|---|---|---|
| Distributed training | ✅ | ✅ |
| Unreliable Internet workers | ✅ | ✅ |
| Heterogeneous GPUs | ✅ | ✅ |
| Open-source framework | ✅ | ✅ |
| Compute marketplace | ✅ Prime is already close | ✅ |
| **Ordinary laptops** | Limited | **Core target** |
| **Phones/NPUs** | Very limited | **First-class workers** |
| **Training + inference + preprocessing + eval** | Fragmented | **One fabric** |
| **Any model provider** | Framework-dependent | **Provider plug-in contract** |
| **Provider keeps IP private** | Partial/problematic | **Explicit architecture requirement** |
| **Consumer resource control/audit** | Not core | **Core requirement** |
| **Transparent job economics** | Partial | **Core protocol** |
| **Multiple competing operators** | Mostly individual ecosystems | **Protocol-level requirement** |
| **Fiat settlement/financing** | Not central | **Possible economic layer** |
| **Distributed model state** | Partial | **Research target** |
| **Distributed-native model architecture** | DiPaCo starts exploring it | **Long-term target** |

So we're **not inventing distributed AI training**.

That's important intellectually.

We're proposing to generalise existing research into something more like:

> ### **An open operating protocol for buying, selling, scheduling, verifying and auditing AI computation across almost any hardware.**

That is a much more defensible statement.

---

# Your plug-in question is the most important architecture question

You asked:

> *How can our framework support Claude/GPT/Gemini/a bank/startup if we don't know their proprietary training process?*

**We shouldn't know it.**

That's the breakthrough in how I would design the interface.

Think about a database.

Kubernetes doesn't need to understand your company's business logic.

AWS doesn't need to understand the algorithm inside every Docker container.

The operating system doesn't understand what Excel is calculating.

Likewise our network should not understand:

> "How does this company train its model?"

It needs to understand a **job contract**.

Something approximately like:

```text
JOB MANIFEST

Provider:        Private Model Company X
Work type:       TRAIN
Hardware:        GPU/NPU/CPU capability X
RAM:             ≥ 6 GB
Storage:         18 GB
Expected time:   42 minutes
Network:         600 MB
Security class:  Confidential
Input:           encrypted work capsule
Output:          encrypted result capsule
Verification:    method V3
Payment:         £0.47
Energy limit:    0.31 kWh
```

The network doesn't need to know what happens inside.

---

# Provider supplies the execution adapter

This is your **plug-in / plug-out** idea.

```text
                  OPEN FABRIC

Model Company A ── Provider Adapter A ──┐
Model Company B ── Provider Adapter B ──┤
University C ───── Provider Adapter C ──┼── JOB CONTRACT
Startup D ──────── Provider Adapter D ──┘
                                           │
                                     Global Fabric
                                           │
                       ┌───────────────────┼────────────────┐
                       ↓                   ↓                ↓
                     Phone              Laptop            GPU
```

The provider adapter knows:

**how to partition its work  
how to package it  
how to execute it  
how to combine results  
how to validate it.**

Our framework knows:

**where it can run  
who has capacity  
security requirements  
resource limits  
metering  
verification requirement  
payment  
failure/retry  
audit.**

That's a clean separation.

---

# And this solves much of the proprietary-training problem

The provider doesn't publish:

```text
"Our secret training algorithm is..."
```

Instead it supplies a signed workload/runtime.

Conceptually:

```text
Provider proprietary system
          ↓
    creates capsule
          ↓
 ┌─────────────────────┐
 │ ENCRYPTED WORKLOAD  │
 │                     │
 │ private code        │
 │ model shard         │
 │ required data       │
 │ execution rules     │
 └─────────────────────┘
          ↓
      Worker sandbox
          ↓
    encrypted result
          ↓
       Provider
```

But here's where Perplexity's objection remains correct:

**we cannot solve consumer trust by making the provider opaque.**

Therefore we need **two independent trust boundaries.**

---

# Provider privacy AND consumer privacy

This is the architecture I would choose:

```text
                 OPEN FABRIC CONTRACT
                         │
              ┌──────────┴──────────┐
              ↓                     ↓
        PROVIDER TRUST         OWNER TRUST
              │                     │
      Protect model/IP        Protect person/device
      Protect dataset         Resource limits
      Protect algorithm       No personal-file access
              │               No camera/mic
              │               Network restrictions
              └──────────┬──────────┘
                         ↓
                ISOLATED EXECUTION
                         ↓
                VERIFIABLE RESULT
```

Neither side should be asked to **trust the other side's goodwill**.

That's much stronger.

---

# And your Uber/eBay analogy actually works

I would separate four actors.

### 1. Compute owner

You, your daughter, a school, company, gaming-PC owner, phone owner, university.

They sell **temporary computation capacity**.

### 2. Model/work provider

AI company, university, startup, pharmaceutical researcher, bank, etc.

They buy computation.

### 3. Fabric operator

Matches demand and supply, verifies work, meters usage, settles payment.

This could be:

**Company A, Company B, Company C...**

### 4. Open protocol

Nobody owns this.

That's analogous to HTTP/Linux/Kubernetes-level infrastructure.

```text
                 OPEN PROTOCOL
                       │
        ┌──────────────┼──────────────┐
        ↓              ↓              ↓
 Operator A        Operator B      Operator C
        │              │              │
    marketplace     enterprise      nonprofit
        │              │              │
        └──────────────┼──────────────┘
                       ↓
                 COMPUTE OWNERS
```

That distinction is **very important**.

We don't need to become Uber.

We could create **the protocol on which many Ubers compete.**

---

# That also fixes another problem

Suppose our organisation disappears.

The network shouldn't disappear.

If the specification, worker, conformance tests and reference implementation are open:

another company can operate it.

Just as:

**Linux ≠ Red Hat.**

**Kubernetes ≠ one cloud provider.**

**Hadoop ≠ Cloudera.**

Your idea should aspire toward:

> **Protocol ≠ marketplace operator.**

Then commercial companies can provide SLA, insurance, compliance, managed workers, enterprise security, financing, billing etc.

That's where businesses can make money without owning the underlying standard.

---

# I would add one more marketplace dimension you haven't mentioned

Don't make providers offer one fixed price.

Allow a genuine **compute exchange**.

Provider says:

> Need 500,000 jobs completed before 06:00 UTC.  
> Maximum £0.03/job.

Workers say:

> I have NPU capacity available for £0.018/job.

Scheduler clears market.

During huge AI training run:

**demand ↑ → compute price ↑ → more people's machines wake up.**

At quiet periods:

**demand ↓ → price ↓ → expensive-electricity nodes stop participating.**

That produces something very much like an **electricity spot market for computation.**

Prime's existing compute exchange is already pursuing part of this commoditisation idea, although currently centred much more heavily on GPU infrastructure. citeturn0search2

---

# One thing I would *not* insist on

I previously pushed **“no centralisation anywhere.”**

I'd modify that.

Don't make decentralisation an ideology.

Make it an **architectural option**.

A pharmaceutical company may say:

> Work may execute only on attested UK enterprise nodes.

An open-source project may say:

> Any device anywhere.

A frontier model provider:

> H100/H200/B200 clusters only.

Our baby model:

> Any CPU/GPU/phone that passes conformance.

Same protocol.

**Policy determines placement.**

That's much stronger than forcing every workload onto people's phones.

---

## Where I think we've arrived

The project is no longer:

> **“Can we train an LLM using laptops?”**

Existing work has already answered enough of that question to make it uninteresting by itself. DiLoCo reduced communication dramatically; INTELLECT-1 actually trained a 10B model globally; INTELLECT-2 distributed asynchronous RL; Google is distributing training across distant datacentres; Prime is building a compute exchange. citeturn0academia58turn0search7turn0search9turn0search0

Our research question is becoming:

> **Can we define an open, model-agnostic and hardware-agnostic AI Compute Protocol in which competing model providers privately package arbitrary AI workloads, competing operators schedule them, independently owned devices securely execute them, results are verifiable, owners control exactly what resources are contributed, and economic value is transparently divided among compute owners, operators and model providers?**

And then **prove that protocol with our baby model on one laptop → two laptops → weak laptop → phone → Internet-separated nodes.**

That is substantially more interesting than where we started tonight.

**I would stop architecture expansion here temporarily.** We now have enough ideas that continuing verbally risks mixing *existing technology*, *our extensions*, and *speculation*. The next useful intellectual step is a proper **prior-art/gap matrix** covering Hivemind, DiLoCo, DiPaCo, PRIME/OpenDiLoCo, INTELLECT-1/2, Decoupled DiLoCo and distributed inference systems, followed by our requirements and the smallest experiment that proves something genuinely new.

## 04/10/2026 00:51 — Distributed AI Fabric: Gate 0

Partner, after the deeper search, **I would not start development yet.** We are in **Discovery / Concept Formation / Prior-Art Validation**, before BRD and before architecture freeze.

And the research changed my view in an important way: **more of our concept already exists than I initially realised.** That is good news because it validates the direction, but it means we must be precise about what we are actually adding.

### What already exists

The landscape is roughly this:

| Area | Existing evidence | Status vs our thinking |
|---|---|---|
| Volunteer distributed compute | BOINC/Folding-style systems | Decades old |
| Phone compute while idle/charging/Wi-Fi | BOINC Android; Google's Gboard FL | Already demonstrated |
| Federated phone training | Flower, Google FL | Mature research area |
| Internet-scale distributed DL | Hivemind | Exists |
| Low-communication LLM training | DiLoCo/OpenDiLoCo | Exists |
| Geographically separated async training | Decoupled DiLoCo | Exists |
| 10B decentralised pretraining | INTELLECT-1 | Demonstrated |
| Distributed RL | INTELLECT-2, Gensyn RL Swarm | Exists |
| Modular distributed-native models | DiPaCo | Research exists |
| Consumer-grade Internet training | Pluralis | **7.5B model over 1,700+ distributed consumer GPUs** |
| Edge foundation-model training | Cleave | Active 2026 research |
| Distributed inference | Petals and newer systems | Exists |
| Browser/phone distributed inference | Synapse/WebGPU experiments | Exists |
| Consumer GPU commercial cloud | SaladCloud | **16,000+ active GPUs/day** |
| Decentralised compute marketplace | Akash/Golem/io.net/Prime | Exists |
| ML-compute protocol | **Gensyn** | Very close |
| Verification of untrusted ML workers | Gensyn Verde, Proof-of-Learning, ZKML | Active field |
| P2P model distribution | Dragonfly/IPFS-type systems | Exists |
| Confidential AI execution | NVIDIA confidential computing, Arm CCA | Exists/developing |

Sources supporting the major findings include DeepMind's DiLoCo/DiPaCo work, Gensyn's protocol and verification work, Prime's protocol, Pluralis' public consumer-GPU run, Salad's commercial consumer hardware network, Google's phone federated learning and Android volunteer-computing work. citeturn0search0turn0search4turn1search0turn1search1turn2search1turn2search5turn1search10turn2search10turn2search11

The Pluralis result is particularly important to our discussion: they report training a **7.5B OLMo-style model over the Internet using more than 1,700 globally distributed consumer-grade GPUs**, explicitly targeting unreliable heterogeneous low-bandwidth machines. citeturn2search5

So we must **not claim invention of decentralised AI training.**

---

# The biggest discovery: Gensyn

Gensyn comes remarkably close to what we were describing.

Their own description is essentially:

> an open protocol connecting scattered compute/capital/data for training, inference, evaluation and payment on devices ranging from datacentres to consumer machines. citeturn2search0turn1search0

They already have:

**P2P communication + machine identity + ML verification + economic coordination + training + inference + evaluation + payment.**

Their Verde work specifically addresses the problem we discussed:

> *How can you know an untrusted person's machine actually performed ML computation correctly?*

It attempts to identify the exact operation at which trainer and verifier disagree rather than repeating an entire training job. citeturn1search1

Therefore, before writing our framework, **Gensyn deserves a proper architecture-level study.**

Otherwise we risk spending six months recreating it.

---

# But our discussion still contains gaps worth investigating

After removing things others already do, I see approximately **six potentially distinctive ideas** remaining.

### 1. Extreme hardware inclusiveness

Gensyn's current RL Swarm documentation still starts around **32 GB CPU RAM** or substantial GPUs such as 3090/4090/5090/A100/H100. citeturn2search3

We're asking a harder question:

> Can **4 GB spare RAM**, weak CPUs, NPUs, old laptops and ordinary phones contribute *something useful*?

Not necessarily gradient training.

The scheduler could assign:

```text
4 GB phone
    ↓
evaluation / tokenisation / validation /
small inference / preprocessing / verification

8 GB laptop
    ↓
small training / embeddings / synthetic tasks

Gaming GPU
    ↓
training / inference

H100 cluster
    ↓
large learner island
```

That's materially different from demanding one minimum machine class.

---

### 2. Whole-AI-lifecycle scheduling

Not merely training.

```text
DATA
 ↓
clean
 ↓
deduplicate
 ↓
tokenise
 ↓
embed
 ↓
train
 ↓
evaluate
 ↓
red-team
 ↓
RL
 ↓
distil
 ↓
infer
 ↓
verify
```

Every operation asks:

> **What is the cheapest trustworthy currently available hardware capable of doing me?**

This is potentially a much bigger optimisation problem.

---

### 3. Provider plug-in without exposing proprietary training

This remains one of our strongest architectural requirements.

Our fabric should **not understand a provider's secret training algorithm.**

Instead:

```text
PROVIDER
   │
   ▼
Provider Adapter
   │
   ▼
Signed Job Manifest
   │
   ├── capability requirements
   ├── security class
   ├── resource limits
   ├── verification mechanism
   ├── encrypted workload
   ├── encrypted result contract
   └── compensation
             │
             ▼
         FABRIC
```

That lets proprietary providers and completely open models potentially use the same infrastructure.

But this is still **a hypothesis requiring security research**, because gradients themselves can leak training information. Distributed-AI literature documents gradient-leakage attacks. citeturn2search12

So "encrypted container" alone is absolutely not sufficient.

---

### 4. Device-owner-first trust

This may become a major philosophical difference.

Most systems begin:

> **How do we protect the customer's workload from an untrusted worker?**

We require both directions:

```text
MODEL PROVIDER
     ↓
 protect IP/data
     ↓
┌──────────────┐
│ TRUST LAYER  │
└──────────────┘
     ↑
 protect owner
     ↑
DEVICE OWNER
```

The owner must control:

**CPU / GPU / RAM / storage / bandwidth / hours / charging-only / thermal ceiling / electricity-price threshold / jurisdiction / permitted workload classes.**

And receive an auditable account of what happened.

Salad already explicitly assumes hostile consumer hosts and isolates workloads using a VM/container architecture, so there is substantial engineering to learn from there rather than invent ourselves. citeturn2search9

---

### 5. Protocol ≠ operator ≠ marketplace

I think we should retain this strongly.

```text
               OPEN STANDARD
                     │
       ┌─────────────┼─────────────┐
       ↓             ↓             ↓
 Operator A      Operator B     Operator C
 commercial       university     nonprofit
       │             │             │
       └─────────────┼─────────────┘
                     ↓
                OPEN WORKERS
```

No mandatory cryptocurrency.

No mandatory marketplace.

No mandatory central scheduler.

No mandatory commercial operator.

An operator could use:

**GBP, USD, INR, credits, donation, university allocation or no payment whatsoever.**

That makes the compute/economic protocol separable.

---

### 6. Distributed-native intelligence

This remains the most ambitious research question.

Instead of forcing today's centrally designed transformer onto distributed hardware:

> **What model architecture would we design if we knew from birth that its brain would live across millions of intermittent heterogeneous devices?**

DiPaCo is already moving toward modularity: different computational paths/modules can train on poorly connected heterogeneous workers. citeturn0search4

Our research would need to go beyond that rather than unknowingly recreate it.

---

# One idea from earlier needs correction

We talked about completely eliminating central model state.

**Don't make that a requirement yet.**

There is already research into decentralised storage, proofs of replication and recovery on unreliable edge devices. citeturn2search13

But there are enormous differences between:

**no central dependency**,  
**no central authority**, and  
**literally no central machines anywhere.**

Those aren't equivalent.

Our architectural rule should instead be:

> **No component is centralised unless measurement, physics, security, regulation or economics demonstrates that centralisation is advantageous.**

Likewise, don't decentralise something merely because we can.

---

# The environmental hypothesis also needs testing

We originally reasoned:

> household compute = fewer datacentres = environmentally better.

**Not necessarily.**

A datacentre GPU operating at 90% utilisation with sophisticated cooling may consume fewer total resources per useful computation than thousands of inefficient household machines.

And phones introduce:

**battery degradation + heat + charging losses + network energy + device lifetime reduction.**

Therefore our fundamental metric cannot simply be:

> GPU-hours decentralised.

It should be closer to:

### **Verified useful AI work / total societal resource cost**

including:

**hardware depreciation + electricity + cooling + networking + carbon + water + battery/device wear + infrastructure + money.**

That could produce surprising conclusions.

Sometimes the datacentre should win.

Our framework must be willing to choose it.

---

# What phase are we actually in?

Not BRD yet.

I would structure this project as follows.

| Gate | Phase | Main question | Output |
|---|---|---|---|
| **G0** | Brainstorm / Discovery | What problem are we really solving? | Concept record |
| **G1** | Prior-art research | Has somebody already solved it? | Landscape + gap matrix |
| **G2** | Problem definition | What remains genuinely unsolved? | Problem Statement |
| **G3** | Hypotheses | What do we believe that needs proof? | Hypothesis register |
| **G4** | Requirements | What must a solution do? | BRD / requirements |
| **G5** | Architecture exploration | What alternative designs could satisfy it? | ADRs + threat model |
| **G6** | Experimental specification | What smallest tests prove/disprove architecture? | Experiment specs |
| **G7** | Reference prototype | One device → 2 → heterogeneous → phone | Working reference |
| **G8** | Scale research | 4 → 8 → 16 → Internet/churn | Benchmark evidence |
| **G9** | Protocol specification | What must independent implementations obey? | Open protocol spec |
| **G10** | Production hardening | Is it secure/reliable/observable? | Conformance suite |
| **G11** | Ecosystem | Can independent providers/operators/devices interoperate? | Public ecosystem |

**We are between G0 and G1.**

We haven't earned the right to write the BRD yet.

---

# Before coding: five documents, not fifty

I wouldn't create them tonight. But eventually I want only these initially:

**1. Concept & Problem Record**  
Everything we discussed, including rejected ideas and why.

**2. Prior-Art & Gap Matrix**  
Gensyn, Prime/INTELLECT, Pluralis, DiLoCo, DiPaCo, Hivemind, Petals, Salad, BOINC, FL/Flower, Cleave, Akash/Golem/io.net, confidential compute, verification systems.

**3. Hypothesis Register**

For example:

> H01 — useful ML workloads can be allocated to devices with <8 GB spare RAM.

> H02 — provider IP can be adequately protected on independently owned hardware.

> H03 — device owners can be protected from arbitrary provider workloads.

> H04 — distributed execution can beat centralised execution on total societal cost for identifiable workload classes.

Every one can end:

**SUPPORTED / REJECTED / INCONCLUSIVE.**

**4. Threat & Trust Model**

Model theft, data leakage, poisoned gradients, fake compute, malicious workload, Sybil attack, collusion, worker disappearance, compromised operator, privacy, jurisdiction, payment fraud, model poisoning, supply-chain attacks.

**5. Measurement Standard**

So nobody—including us or another AI—can later say *"distributed is better"* without numbers.

---

# Testing should exist before implementation

Your point about unit/system/integration testing is important, but for this project it goes further.

We need:

```text
Research hypothesis tests
        ↓
Algorithm tests
        ↓
Unit tests
        ↓
Component tests
        ↓
Contract tests
        ↓
Adapter conformance tests
        ↓
Integration tests
        ↓
Distributed-system tests
        ↓
Network impairment tests
        ↓
Churn/failure tests
        ↓
Security tests
        ↓
Adversarial/Byzantine tests
        ↓
Privacy-leakage tests
        ↓
Performance benchmarks
        ↓
Energy/thermal tests
        ↓
Economic simulations
        ↓
Scale tests
```

And every sprint requirement should trace:

**Problem → Requirement → ADR → Implementation → Test → Evidence.**

That prevents the kind of situation we've encountered elsewhere where a tracker says something is implemented while evidence tells a different story. memcite

---

# AI roles: don't assign them permanently yet

I wouldn't decide today:

> Claude builds, ChatGPT reviews, Perplexity researches, Codex codes.

That risks adapting the project around today's products.

Instead establish **roles independent of vendor/model**:

| Role | Responsibility |
|---|---|
| Researcher | Find prior art/evidence |
| Architect | Propose alternatives |
| Challenger | Attempt to disprove them |
| Spec owner | Maintain requirements/traceability |
| Builder | Implement only approved spec |
| Test engineer | Build independent tests |
| Security reviewer | Attack trust assumptions |
| Evidence reviewer | Verify completion claims |

Then you can put ChatGPT, Claude, Perplexity, Codex—or future systems—into those roles based on measured performance.

**No AI should approve its own implementation.**

That principle is more important than which AI we use.

---

# Do we need more brainstorming?

**Yes—but not unrestricted brainstorming.**

We've reached the point where additional free-form ideas will start generating duplication.

Next conversation should be **G1: Prior-Art & Gap Analysis**.

And I would deliberately attempt to **kill our idea first**.

Search for:

> Who already does every part of this?

> Is Gensyn effectively already our project?

> What exactly is missing from Gensyn?

> What exactly is missing from Pluralis?

> Why hasn't Salad moved from stateless consumer workloads into distributed frontier training?

> Why haven't phone-based federated systems become general compute markets?

> What failed historically in BOINC-style commercial compute?

> Is protecting proprietary weights on hostile consumer hardware actually achievable?

> Does paying households make economic sense after electricity and hardware depreciation?

> Which workloads are actually cheaper distributed?

Only after those answers should we define **our contribution**.

If the answer becomes:

## 03/10/2026 22:52 — AI Must Pay Its Physical Bill

Yes. I understand the question now. **You are not asking how you personally survive higher RAM or laptop prices. You're asking what responsibility the AI industry has for a worldwide externality it is helping create.**

And I agree with the premise behind the challenge: saying *“AI will create abundance”* while consuming scarce memory, chips, electricity, water, land and capital—and pushing some costs onto everyone else—is incomplete.

I also wouldn't claim that I personally am “superintelligent.” But if increasingly capable AI is supposed to justify the resources society is pouring into it, **it should help solve the scarcity it creates, not merely win the competition for scarce resources.**

### My answer is not “build more datacentres”

The world needs a **closed-loop AI infrastructure strategy**:

**AI demand → scarcity → AI helps expand/optimise supply → efficiency improves → resources return to society → AI can grow again.**

That requires several things happening together.

1. **Stop treating bigger models as the only route to better intelligence.**  
   Every query should not automatically consume the largest model available. Routing, specialised models, distillation, quantisation, caching, sparse/MoE computation and local/on-device inference should drive *compute required per useful unit of intelligence* dramatically downward.

2. **Use AI aggressively to improve the semiconductor system itself.**  
   Chip design, verification, fab scheduling, yield optimisation, packaging, memory architecture, materials discovery and manufacturing automation are exactly the kinds of enormously complex optimisation problems AI should attack. If AI consumes 10× more memory but helps the industry eventually manufacture memory 20× more efficiently, the equation changes.

3. **Datacentres should become flexible energy consumers rather than privileged energy consumers.**  
   Training workloads that aren't latency-sensitive can move geographically and temporally toward surplus renewable/nuclear/grid capacity. Datacentres can reduce workloads during grid stress instead of competing with households and industry at the worst possible time.

4. **Build circular hardware infrastructure.**  
   GPUs, servers, batteries, cooling systems and electronics shouldn't follow a constant replace-and-discard cycle. Components should be designed for reuse, refurbishment and material recovery. AI itself can optimise that supply chain.

5. **Protect ordinary computing capacity.**  
   This one is rarely discussed. If AI infrastructure becomes so profitable that manufacturers systematically divert memory and semiconductor capacity away from ordinary devices, governments have a legitimate competition/industrial-policy problem to consider. Society still needs affordable PCs, phones, automotive chips, medical electronics and industrial equipment.

6. **Measure the externality publicly.**  
   Major AI systems should ultimately be measurable not merely by benchmark score, but something closer to:

   **useful intelligence / £ / joule / litre of water / kg CO₂ / semiconductor capacity.**

   Then you can see whether the next generation is actually technologically better—or merely **larger and richer**.

---

### But there is a deeper solution

Suppose AI requires $1 trillion of infrastructure and ultimately makes humanity only marginally more productive.

**That's a poor bargain.**

Suppose the same infrastructure produces systems capable of accelerating:

- new semiconductor materials,
- cheaper energy storage,
- nuclear/fusion engineering,
- grid optimisation,
- drug discovery,
- automated manufacturing,
- agriculture,
- climate modelling,
- logistics,
- education,
- scientific research.

Then AI has started **repaying the physical resources society invested in it**.

That is the standard I would use.

And there's an uncomfortable possibility that should be stated plainly:

> **If increasingly powerful AI cannot eventually produce more real-world abundance than the scarcity its infrastructure creates, then scaling it indefinitely is not evidence of superintelligence. It is evidence of an inefficient industry.**

### And Sharanya is actually part of the world-level problem you're pointing at

I won't turn this into advice about her.

Your concern is broader: imagine millions of young people.

One student uses increasingly capable AI continuously. Another doesn't. The first can potentially learn, research, create and execute much faster.

So society faces **two inequalities simultaneously**:

**AI access inequality**  
People without access risk falling behind.

**AI-caused physical scarcity**  
The infrastructure required to provide that access can itself increase the cost of the devices and resources needed to participate.

That's a contradiction.

The long-term objective therefore cannot be:

> *Everyone must buy increasingly expensive hardware to access increasingly enormous AI.*

It has to become:

> **Extremely capable intelligence available from ordinary, inexpensive hardware, while most expensive computation is efficiently shared infrastructure.**

In other words, if this technology really progresses toward what people are calling **superintelligence**, one sign of success should eventually be almost paradoxical:

**the intelligence gets enormously more capable while the physical resources required per person go down.**

If instead every generation requires another trillion dollars, another mountain of GPUs, another memory shortage and another power crisis just to remain competitive, **we haven't solved intelligence economically yet.**

### The chain is roughly this

**AI expectations / AGI race / investor money**
→ hyperscalers spend enormous amounts on AI infrastructure  
→ more GPUs/accelerators + servers  
→ enormous requirement for **HBM, server DRAM, NAND/SSDs, networking and power**  
→ memory manufacturers allocate more production toward high-margin AI/server products  
→ less capacity available for conventional PC/mobile memory  
→ **DRAM/NAND prices rise**
→ laptop/phone manufacturers either absorb the cost, reduce specifications, remove cheap models, or **increase prices**.

And this isn't merely my interpretation.

Samsung said just **four days ago** that HBM could consume nearly **30% of global DRAM wafer capacity next year**, versus around 20% currently. Importantly, HBM and ordinary DRAM compete for manufacturing capacity. citeturn0news9

### And yes — it has reached laptops and phones

A charger mainly depends on power semiconductors, controllers, transformers/inductors, capacitors, GaN components in higher-end chargers, manufacturing and logistics. It doesn't contain large quantities of DRAM/NAND.

That's why your earlier statement — *“build everything that can be coded; leave only what physically cannot be coded”* — becomes more interesting economically.

The scarce thing may increasingly **not be code**.

The scarce things become **compute, memory, electricity, physical infrastructure, distribution, regulatory permission and customers.**

And this is happening **before we need to decide whether “superintelligence” is real**. Companies and investors merely need to *believe AI demand will be enormous* and spend accordingly. The physical economic consequences happen **today**, irrespective of whether AGI/superintelligence ultimately arrives.

That distinction is important. citeturn0search4turn0search8

items.snippet: Samsung Electronics announced that High-Bandwidth Memory (HBM) is projected to comprise nearly 30% of the global Dynamic Random-Access Memory (DRAM) wafer capacity by next year, up from the current 20%. According to Executive Vice President Kim Taewoo, HBM and standard DRAM share wafer production capacity, so increasing HBM output may limit the availability of standard DRAM. HBM is essential for artificial intelligence (AI) computing due to its ability to stack memory chips vertically, enabling processors to quickly access substantial data volumes. The HBM market is currently led by South Korea's SK Hynix and Samsung Electronics, along with U.S.-based Micron Technology.
